screens.title: Logging, Monitoring, and System Performance
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we build a practical habit for observing and diagnosing Linux systems. You will learn how modern distributions record events in a binary systemd journal and how traditional plain-text logs in /var/log still provide critical evidence. We will also cover tools that reveal C P U, memory, disk, and network health, and a simple workflow for turning noisy symptoms into targeted action. For example, you will see how a high input and output wait value suggests disk contention and how the iostat command helps confirm that hypothesis. You will practice rotating growing logs with logrotate so logs don’t exhaust disk space. This matters because effective troubleshooting begins with reliable data: accurate logs and timely performance metrics. By the end of this chapter you will be able to find relevant messages, limit log growth, run quick checks for resource pressure, and follow a stepwise diagnostic process. As you go, notice common pitfalls such as checking the wrong log file, misconfigured logrotate permissions, or monitoring with tools that themselves create load. Keep these habits: find the right logs, verify the resource, then act.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: We start by making clear, measurable learning objectives you can practice. First, locate and interpret system logs using journalctl and classic text viewers; this skill helps you find the timeline of an incident and confirm whether a service failed, restarted, or reported errors. Second, configure logrotate to keep logs from growing out of control; managing log retention prevents full disks and lost diagnostics. Third, use command-line monitoring tools such as top, htop, free, df, du, iostat, and vmstat to collect real-time metrics that reveal where the system is constrained. Fourth, analyze those metrics to identify bottlenecks in C P U, memory, disk input and output, and network so you can determine whether to optimize, extend resources, or throttle workloads. Each objective pairs a command with a purpose: read the data, decide the root cause, and act in a way that preserves service. These are practical, repeatable skills you’ll use in incident response and day-to-day maintenance. Practice them in a safe environment and note common misconceptions, like trusting free memory instead of available memory or rotating logs without correct permissions.

screens.title: Systemd Journal vs Traditional Text Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Start by understanding the two main log sources on modern Linux systems and why both matter. The systemd journal is a binary store managed by systemd-journald. It captures kernel messages, system services, and structured metadata. You query it with journalctl, which offers fast filters by service, priority, and time range. For example, asking for a unit’s recent error messages narrows your search to only the service you care about and avoids noise from unrelated messages. Traditional plain-text logs live under /var/log and include syslog or messages, auth logs, kernel logs, and application-specific files like webserver access and error logs. These files are human-readable and portable. Use tail, less, and grep against /var/log when you need immediate line-based context or when systemd journal is not available. A common misconception is that the journal replaces older logs entirely; in practice, many applications continue to write text logs and administrators often need both sources. A practical example: if a web application crashes, you might use journalctl -u the-service to see service restarts, then tail -f /var/log/apache2/error. log to see application errors. The key takeaway is to treat the journal as a structured timeline and /var/log as complementary, persistent records you can archive and rotate.

keyIdea.title: Two complementary sources
keyIdea.text: Use journalctl for structured, service-focused queries and /var/log text files for legacy and application-specific messages.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Journal vs Text Logs
Journalctl (systemd journal)
Structured, binary journal ideal for service-focused queries and time filters.
journalctl -f
journalctl -u sshd
journalctl --since "2023-01-01 10:00:00" --until "2023-01-01 10:15:00"
journalctl -p err
• Use unit filters to limit output to a specific service.
• Use priority filters to focus on errors or warnings only.
• The journal stores metadata that aids correlation across services.
Key Takeaway

Journalctl is your first stop for service timelines and structured queries; it complements text logs.

Traditional /var/log files
Plain-text logs for kernel, auth, and application output—human readable and portable.
tail -f /var/log/syslog
less /var/log/auth.log
grep "error" /var/log/apache2/error.log
• Use tail -f to follow live writes from services that write to text logs.
• Grep and less help extract lines and context when investigating an incident.
• Keep these logs rotated and compressed to avoid filling disks.
Common Mistake

Relying on free memory instead of available memory leads to false conclusions about memory pressure.

screens.title: Using journalctl: Filters and Time Ranges
screens.narratorSegment: Journalctl becomes powerful when you apply precise filters. Start by identifying the unit name of the service you care about. Asking for that unit’s logs with a unit filter limits the output to relevant lines and saves time. Priority filtering narrows entries to levels like err or warning so you focus on actionable events. Time range filters let you isolate a window around the incident. For example, combining unit, priority, and time produces a concise set of error messages to inspect. A concrete example: if the SSH service restarted unexpectedly at 10:05, use a time range around that timestamp and ask only for err priority. This reduces thousands of lines to a handful of useful records. A frequent misconception is that broader queries are safer; in reality they often hide the needle in too much hay. Another issue is forgetting timezone or system clock differences when picking a time window; confirm the system clock first. Practice queries such as journalctl -u sshd -p err --since "2023-01-01 10:00:00" --until "2023-01-01 10:15:00" and compare results with tail -f on the corresponding /var/log file when available. The skill here is iterative narrowing: start broad, then add unit, priority, and time until you have a manageable set of entries you can interpret.

keyIdea.title: Precision querying
keyIdea.text: Combine unit, priority, and time filters to quickly find the exact messages that explain an event.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › journalctl Filters
Filter Patterns
Examples that you will practice to narrow results quickly.
journalctl -u sshd
journalctl -f
journalctl -p err
journalctl --since "2023-01-01 10:00:00" --until "2023-01-01 10:15:00"
journalctl -u nginx -p warning --since "1 hour ago"
• Use -u to scope to a service unit name.
• Use -p for priority to focus on warnings or errors.
• Use relative times like "1 hour ago" for convenience during live incidents.
Common Pitfalls & Tips
Avoid broad queries and check the system clock if time ranges seem off.
Tip
Start with a unit filter, then add priority and a short time window to keep output manageable.
Example Walkthrough
If a user reports a failed login at 14:22, run journalctl -u sshd --since "14:20" --until "14:25" -p err to see related authentication errors and confirm the cause.

screens.title: Plain-Text Logs and File Locations
screens.narratorSegment: Plain-text log files remain an essential source of truth because many applications write directly to files under /var/log. Know the usual filenames so you can find the right conversation quickly. On Debian-based systems, /var/log/syslog collects general system messages; on Red Hat variants the same role is often filled by /var/log/messages. Authentication events are found in /var/log/auth. log or /var/log/secure depending on distribution. Kernel messages and boot diagnostics appear in /var/log/kern. log and /var/log/dmesg. Web servers maintain access and error logs in directories such as /var/log/apache2. Use simple tools to read them: cat for a quick dump, less for paged reading, grep to filter lines of interest, and tail -f to watch live writes during a reproduction. For example, when diagnosing an authentication failure, grep the auth log for a username and then tail -f while you reproduce an attempt to observe live error messages. A common misconception is that only the journal holds authoritative data; text logs often include application-level context that the journal may not. Maintain permissions when accessing logs—insufficient privileges can hide entries. Finally, keep your mental map of filenames—when you see an error from an application, check both the journal and its dedicated text log to get both system-level and application-level context.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › /var/log Locations
Common Files
  • /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages — general system activity
  • /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure — authentication and security events
  • /var/log/kern.log and /var/log/dmesg — kernel and boot messages

tail -f /var/log/syslog
less /var/log/auth.log
grep -i "failure" /var/log/apache2/error.log
Reading Tips
Use tail -f during reproduction and grep to extract candidate lines for faster analysis.
Pro Tip
Confirm file ownership and permissions before assuming a log is empty; lack of read access can hide entries.
Key Takeaway

Pair journalctl timelines with text logs to gain both system-level sequence and application-specific context.

screens.title: Log Rotation with logrotate
screens.narratorSegment: Logrotate automates archiving and pruning of log files so logs do not consume all available disk space. Its main configuration lives in /etc/logrotate. conf and includes per-service snippets in /etc/logrotate. d. Each block controls when to rotate, how many archives to keep, whether to compress, and any service-specific actions to run after rotation. A typical Apache example rotates weekly, keeps four archived logs, compresses old ones, and tells Apache to reload its configuration so it will open the newly created files. Common pitfalls include incorrect paths in the block, insufficient permissions to create rotated files, and failing to reload or restart the service gracefully, which can cause the application to keep writing to the old, removed file. To validate a configuration, use a forced run: logrotate -f /etc/logrotate. conf and then confirm new compressed files exist and that the service continues logging. A concrete example block is included in the visual; read it, then run a forced rotate in a safe test environment and check that access and error logs are rotated as expected. The key skill is writing precise paths and verifying postrotate steps so that rotation does not interrupt logging.

keyIdea.title: Safe rotation
keyIdea.text: Logrotate reduces disk use; always test a new configuration with a forced run and confirm service reload behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › logrotate Basics
Sample Configuration
This example shows a common Apache logrotate block and its directives.
/var/log/apache2/*.log {
    weekly
    missingok
    rotate 4
    compress
    delaycompress
    notifempty
    create 0640 root adm
    sharedscripts
    postrotate
        /etc/init.d/apache2 reload > /dev/null
    endscript
}
Key directives: rotate controls retention, compress saves space, create sets permissions, postrotate runs commands after rotation.
Validation & Pitfalls
Always force a rotate in a safe environment to validate paths and postrotate behavior.
Common Mistakes
  • Wrong path globs that never match logs.
  • Permissions in create preventing service from writing to new files.
  • Not reloading service, causing logging to continue on removed files.
Check

Run logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.conf and confirm new rotated files and service log continuity.

screens.title: CPU Monitoring: top, htop, and mpstat
screens.narratorSegment: C P U monitoring tools tell you which processes consume time and whether the C P U is waiting on input and output. Use top or htop for an immediate, per-process view: these show C P U percentage per process and a summary line for system, user, and iowait times. A high iowait value, often labeled wa in top, indicates the C P U is idle while waiting for disk operations to complete—this often points to a disk input and output bottleneck rather than C P U saturation. Mpstat and similar utilities report per-processor statistics across intervals and are useful when you suspect uneven load across cores. A concrete example: if top shows low user and system C P U percentages but wa at 40–50%, the C P U is often idle because it is waiting for disk reads or writes; the next step is to run iostat to inspect disk utilization. A common misconception is to kill the top C P U consumer immediately; if iowait is the cause, killing a C P U-bound process may not resolve the underlying disk contention. Practice identifying the symptoms: find the process list in top, note overall iowait, and correlate with iostat to find the busy device. This combination gives you evidence to choose whether to throttle processes, change input and output scheduling, or provision faster storage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › CPU Monitoring
top / htop
Real-time process view. Look at user, system, and wa (I/O wait).
# Run top or htop and observe the summary line for:
# - %us (user)
# - %sy (system)
# - %wa (iowait)
# High %wa suggests disk I/O contention
mpstat
Reports per-CPU usage over time for deeper patterns.
Practical Rule
If top shows high wa, run iostat to determine which device is responsible before killing processes.
Key Takeaway

Distinguish between CPU-bound and I/O-bound symptoms: iowait points to disk work, not CPU cycles.

screens.title: Memory Monitoring with free and vmstat
screens.narratorSegment: Memory monitoring focuses on whether processes have sufficient R A M and whether the system is swapping. Use free -h to see total, used, and available memory; 'available' is the practical metric for how much memory the kernel can use for new allocations. A common mistake is to look only at free memory and conclude there is a problem when the kernel has cached memory that it will release as needed. Vmstat gives a broader picture: it reports processes, memory, swap, block input and output, and C P U fields including si and so—swap in and swap out. High si/so values show heavy swapping and indicate memory pressure or leaks. For example, a server that shows low available memory and rising swap activity is likely experiencing sustained memory pressure that will slow performance. The right reaction is to find leaking processes or add memory, not merely to clear caches. A practical approach: run free -h to check available memory, then vmstat to see if si/so values are elevated; if swap activity is high, find the process consuming memory and consider restarting or optimizing it. Be mindful that aggressive monitoring intervals can themselves affect behavior; collect short samples during investigation and avoid long-running, resource-heavy sampling on production hosts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Memory Monitoring
free -h
Shows total, used, free, and available memory with human-readable units.
free -h
# Focus on 'available' not just 'free' to judge memory for new allocations
vmstat
Reports processes, memory, swap, block I/O, and CPU activity, including si/so.
Interpretation
High si/so indicates swapping. If swapping is frequent, identify and fix the memory-hungry process or add RAM.
Key Takeaway

Check available memory and vmstat's swap fields; sustained swapping degrades performance.

screens.title: Disk I/O Monitoring: df, du and iostat
screens.narratorSegment: Disk issues often show up as full filesystems or as slow input and output that makes applications wait. Start with df -h to find filesystems that are nearly full; a full root filesystem can prevent services from writing logs and crash processes. Use du -sh on suspect directories to find large files or folders eating space. For live performance, iostat reports per-device read/write throughput, utilization percent, and await times; high %util and high await mean the device is busy and requests are waiting. For example, if df -h shows adequate space but top shows high iowait, run iostat -xz 1 to watch utilization and await across devices. Look at r/s and w/s to see read and write request rates and %util to see how saturated the device is. A common misconception is equating large file counts with slow input and output; the device's utilization and average wait time are the real indicators. After identifying a busy device, inspect which processes are performing heavy input and output and consider throttling, scheduling, or moving data off the device. Remember that heavy monitoring itself can produce additional input and output, so use short, targeted sampling intervals when diagnosing production systems.

narration.text: Disk issues often show up as full filesystems or as slow input and output that makes applications wait. Start with df -h to find filesystems that are nearly full; a full root filesystem can prevent services from writing logs and crash processes. Use du -sh on suspect directories to find large files or folders eating space. For live performance, iostat reports per-device read/write throughput, utilization percent, and await times; high %util and high await mean the device is busy and requests are waiting. For example, if df -h shows adequate space but top shows high iowait, run iostat -xz 1 to watch utilization and await across devices. Look at r/s and w/s to see read and write request rates and %util to see how saturated the device is. A common misconception is equating large file counts with slow input and output; the device's utilization and average wait time are the real indicators. After identifying a busy device, inspect which processes are performing heavy input and output and consider throttling, scheduling, or moving data off the device. Remember that heavy monitoring itself can produce additional input and output, so use short, targeted sampling intervals when diagnosing production systems.

keyIdea.title: Disk Signals
keyIdea.text: Use df/du to find space issues and iostat to measure device load and average wait times to confirm I/O bottlenecks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Disk I/O
Space Checks: df & du
Find full filesystems and large directories that may cause problems.
df -h /
du -sh /var/log
# If root is full, logs may not be written and services can fail
iostat for Performance
Measure reads/writes, utilization, and await to confirm a device bottleneck.
iostat -xz 1
# Watch %util and await. High values indicate device saturation and long waits.
Key Takeaway

Confirm disk saturation with iostat before changing process behavior; freeing space and reducing I/O often reduces iowait.

screens.title: Network Tools for Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Network performance problems can mimic other bottlenecks, so include a network check in your diagnostic flow. Use ss -s or netstat -s for a summary of connection statistics and errors; these help reveal retransmits, dropped packets, or unusually high connection counts. Tools like iftop or nload provide per-interface bandwidth usage when installed and are useful for live observation of traffic spikes. ip -s link shows transmit and receive statistics including errors and dropped packets for each interface. As an example, if users complain about slowness and all local metrics look normal, check ip -s link to see if an interface is reporting dropped packets, then run iftop to observe which host is generating large traffic. A common misconception is to equate bandwidth saturation with server load; often errors and dropped packets cause retransmits and appear as high apparent load. Always check both errors and bandwidth. Remember that iftop and similar tools are not always installed by default and may require privileges; use them briefly on production systems to reduce tool overhead. Correlate network findings with application logs to determine whether slowness originates from networking or from a busy backend.

ss -s
ip -s link
# Check for errors, dropped packets, and interface statistics

Use iftop or nload to see which hosts or processes are using bandwidth.

screens.title: Systematic Troubleshooting Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When a server is slow, follow a short, repeatable workflow to reduce guesswork. Start with top or htop to see if C P U, memory, or iowait dominates. If C P U is high, identify the top process consuming C P U and ask whether that load is expected. If memory looks low, check free -h and vmstat for swapping; high si/so indicates memory pressure. If top shows high iowait, run iostat to inspect disk device utilization and await times to find a busy disk. If the filesystem is full, run df -h and du -sh on large directories to free space. For network concerns, check ss -s and ip -s link, then iftop for live bandwidth. Always consult logs with journalctl or relevant /var/log files to add event context—logs often explain whether a service failed or restarted. The workflow is iterative: observe, hypothesize, test with the appropriate tool, and act. For example, if you see high iowait and iostat reports high %util on /dev/sda, identify IO-heavy processes, stop or limit them, and clean up large file writes. The advantage of a consistent workflow is that it converges on a root cause quickly and reduces unnecessary changes during incidents.

keyIdea.title: Observe → Hypothesize → Test → Act
keyIdea.text: A short, repeatable workflow saves time and avoids knee-jerk changes that can worsen incidents.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Troubleshooting Workflow
Step-by-step
1 Observe
Run top/htop to identify dominant resource usage.
2 Hypothesize
Is it CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network? Form a testable hypothesis.
3 Test
Run vmstat, iostat, df, ss or journalctl as appropriate to confirm.
4 Act
Throttle, restart, rotate logs, free space, or provision resources based on evidence.
A lean workflow minimizes changes during incidents and helps you gather the right evidence for long-term fixes.
Check Your Understanding

Given high iowait but low user CPU, which command would you run next to confirm the disk device at fault?

screens.title: Simulating a Disk I/O Load and Live Diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario reproduces disk write pressure and walks you through live diagnosis. In a safe test environment, generate a large file with dd to simulate heavy writes. For example, dd if=/dev/zero of=largefile bs=1M count=1000 conv=fdatasync & launches a background write load. While the dd command runs, observe C P U and memory with top or htop and watch the summary line for wa—high values indicate waiting on input and output. Next, run iostat -xz 2 5 to sample device statistics and focus on %util and await; rising %util and long await times confirm the disk is saturated. Check df -h / to ensure the filesystem has space and du -sh largefile to confirm file size. While the load runs, monitor logs with journalctl -f -p err and in another terminal tail -f /var/log/syslog (or /var/log/messages) to catch any disk-related kernel errors. After you finish, remove the generated file with rm largefile. A common misconception is to conclude that the slow process is C P U-bound; this exercise shows how high iowait with low user C P U indicates disk saturation, and iostat gives the numeric proof you can present as evidence.

keyIdea.title: Reproduce to Observe
keyIdea.text: Simulating load and sampling iostat and logs in parallel lets you correlate symptoms to the device and avoid wrong conclusions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Hands-on Demo
Simulate & Diagnose
# Simulate heavy disk writes (run in a test shell)
dd if=/dev/zero of=largefile bs=1M count=1000 conv=fdatasync &

# Monitor CPU/memory
top
free -h

# Sample disk stats
iostat -xz 2 5

# Check space
df -h /
du -sh largefile

# Monitor logs
journalctl -f -p err
# or
tail -f /var/log/syslog

# Cleanup
rm largefile
Observation
High wa in top with high %util and await in iostat confirms the disk is the bottleneck.
Misconception Alert
Do not assume a busy process is CPU-bound—check iostat to verify device saturation first.
Key Takeaway

Simulate load, observe metrics, and confirm with logs to make evidence-based remediation decisions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core things to remember. First, logs are your primary evidence; use journalctl for structured, service-centric queries and /var/log text files for application-level context. Second, logrotate protects disk space: write precise rules, test with a forced run, and verify service reload behavior. Third, monitoring tools are diagnostic sensors: top and htop show per-process usage and iowait, free and vmstat reveal memory pressure and swapping, iostat quantifies device utilization and wait times, and network summaries and live bandwidth tools highlight network issues. Fourth, follow a concise troubleshooting workflow: observe, hypothesize, test with the right tool, and act. These core concepts are connected—logs provide events, metrics provide resource state, and a workflow ties them together so you can take effective action. Keep practicing the sample tasks and the hands-on scenario to build quick pattern recognition. Which signal will you check first the next time your server feels slow?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we build a practical habit for observing and diagnosing Linux systems. You will learn how modern distributions record events in a binary systemd journal and how traditional plain-text logs in /var/log still provide critical evidence. We will also cover tools that reveal C P U, memory, disk, and network health, and a simple workflow for turning noisy symptoms into targeted action. For example, you will see how a high input and output wait value suggests disk contention and how the iostat command helps confirm that hypothesis. You will practice rotating growing logs with logrotate so logs don’t exhaust disk space. This matters because effective troubleshooting begins with reliable data: accurate logs and timely performance metrics. By the end of this chapter you will be able to find relevant messages, limit log growth, run quick checks for resource pressure, and follow a stepwise diagnostic process. As you go, notice common pitfalls such as checking the wrong log file, misconfigured logrotate permissions, or monitoring with tools that themselves create load. Keep these habits: find the right logs, verify the resource, then act.

We start by making clear, measurable learning objectives you can practice. First, locate and interpret system logs using journalctl and classic text viewers; this skill helps you find the timeline of an incident and confirm whether a service failed, restarted, or reported errors. Second, configure logrotate to keep logs from growing out of control; managing log retention prevents full disks and lost diagnostics. Third, use command-line monitoring tools such as top, htop, free, df, du, iostat, and vmstat to collect real-time metrics that reveal where the system is constrained. Fourth, analyze those metrics to identify bottlenecks in C P U, memory, disk input and output, and network so you can determine whether to optimize, extend resources, or throttle workloads. Each objective pairs a command with a purpose: read the data, decide the root cause, and act in a way that preserves service. These are practical, repeatable skills you’ll use in incident response and day-to-day maintenance. Practice them in a safe environment and note common misconceptions, like trusting free memory instead of available memory or rotating logs without correct permissions.

These practice objectives give you small, testable tasks during the hands-on demo. First, filter the systemd journal by service and severity; this teaches precise queries so you do not chase irrelevant messages. Second, practice rotating a webserver log using a sample logrotate file and a forced run to observe rotation and service reload behavior. Third, run iostat and interpret percent utilization and await to recognize disk bottlenecks. Fourth, set up a simple monitoring checklist: check top for C P U and iowait, free for available memory, df for filesystem fullness, and ss for network errors. Each practice objective maps a command to a verification step — for example, after rotating logs, confirm the service still writes to the new file. These tasks reduce guessing and help you form hypotheses you can confirm with data. Remember that monitoring tools have overhead, so use them judiciously on production systems and prefer short sampling windows for diagnostics.

Start by understanding the two main log sources on modern Linux systems and why both matter. The systemd journal is a binary store managed by systemd-journald. It captures kernel messages, system services, and structured metadata. You query it with journalctl, which offers fast filters by service, priority, and time range. For example, asking for a unit’s recent error messages narrows your search to only the service you care about and avoids noise from unrelated messages. Traditional plain-text logs live under /var/log and include syslog or messages, auth logs, kernel logs, and application-specific files like webserver access and error logs. These files are human-readable and portable. Use tail, less, and grep against /var/log when you need immediate line-based context or when systemd journal is not available. A common misconception is that the journal replaces older logs entirely; in practice, many applications continue to write text logs and administrators often need both sources. A practical example: if a web application crashes, you might use journalctl -u the-service to see service restarts, then tail -f /var/log/apache2/error. log to see application errors. The key takeaway is to treat the journal as a structured timeline and /var/log as complementary, persistent records you can archive and rotate.

Journalctl becomes powerful when you apply precise filters. Start by identifying the unit name of the service you care about. Asking for that unit’s logs with a unit filter limits the output to relevant lines and saves time. Priority filtering narrows entries to levels like err or warning so you focus on actionable events. Time range filters let you isolate a window around the incident. For example, combining unit, priority, and time produces a concise set of error messages to inspect. A concrete example: if the SSH service restarted unexpectedly at 10:05, use a time range around that timestamp and ask only for err priority. This reduces thousands of lines to a handful of useful records. A frequent misconception is that broader queries are safer; in reality they often hide the needle in too much hay. Another issue is forgetting timezone or system clock differences when picking a time window; confirm the system clock first. Practice queries such as journalctl -u sshd -p err --since "2023-01-01 10:00:00" --until "2023-01-01 10:15:00" and compare results with tail -f on the corresponding /var/log file when available. The skill here is iterative narrowing: start broad, then add unit, priority, and time until you have a manageable set of entries you can interpret.

Plain-text log files remain an essential source of truth because many applications write directly to files under /var/log. Know the usual filenames so you can find the right conversation quickly. On Debian-based systems, /var/log/syslog collects general system messages; on Red Hat variants the same role is often filled by /var/log/messages. Authentication events are found in /var/log/auth. log or /var/log/secure depending on distribution. Kernel messages and boot diagnostics appear in /var/log/kern. log and /var/log/dmesg. Web servers maintain access and error logs in directories such as /var/log/apache2. Use simple tools to read them: cat for a quick dump, less for paged reading, grep to filter lines of interest, and tail -f to watch live writes during a reproduction. For example, when diagnosing an authentication failure, grep the auth log for a username and then tail -f while you reproduce an attempt to observe live error messages. A common misconception is that only the journal holds authoritative data; text logs often include application-level context that the journal may not. Maintain permissions when accessing logs—insufficient privileges can hide entries. Finally, keep your mental map of filenames—when you see an error from an application, check both the journal and its dedicated text log to get both system-level and application-level context.

Logrotate automates archiving and pruning of log files so logs do not consume all available disk space. Its main configuration lives in /etc/logrotate. conf and includes per-service snippets in /etc/logrotate. d. Each block controls when to rotate, how many archives to keep, whether to compress, and any service-specific actions to run after rotation. A typical Apache example rotates weekly, keeps four archived logs, compresses old ones, and tells Apache to reload its configuration so it will open the newly created files. Common pitfalls include incorrect paths in the block, insufficient permissions to create rotated files, and failing to reload or restart the service gracefully, which can cause the application to keep writing to the old, removed file. To validate a configuration, use a forced run: logrotate -f /etc/logrotate. conf and then confirm new compressed files exist and that the service continues logging. A concrete example block is included in the visual; read it, then run a forced rotate in a safe test environment and check that access and error logs are rotated as expected. The key skill is writing precise paths and verifying postrotate steps so that rotation does not interrupt logging.

C P U monitoring tools tell you which processes consume time and whether the C P U is waiting on input and output. Use top or htop for an immediate, per-process view: these show C P U percentage per process and a summary line for system, user, and iowait times. A high iowait value, often labeled wa in top, indicates the C P U is idle while waiting for disk operations to complete—this often points to a disk input and output bottleneck rather than C P U saturation. Mpstat and similar utilities report per-processor statistics across intervals and are useful when you suspect uneven load across cores. A concrete example: if top shows low user and system C P U percentages but wa at 40–50%, the C P U is often idle because it is waiting for disk reads or writes; the next step is to run iostat to inspect disk utilization. A common misconception is to kill the top C P U consumer immediately; if iowait is the cause, killing a C P U-bound process may not resolve the underlying disk contention. Practice identifying the symptoms: find the process list in top, note overall iowait, and correlate with iostat to find the busy device. This combination gives you evidence to choose whether to throttle processes, change input and output scheduling, or provision faster storage.

Memory monitoring focuses on whether processes have sufficient R A M and whether the system is swapping. Use free -h to see total, used, and available memory; 'available' is the practical metric for how much memory the kernel can use for new allocations. A common mistake is to look only at free memory and conclude there is a problem when the kernel has cached memory that it will release as needed. Vmstat gives a broader picture: it reports processes, memory, swap, block input and output, and C P U fields including si and so—swap in and swap out. High si/so values show heavy swapping and indicate memory pressure or leaks. For example, a server that shows low available memory and rising swap activity is likely experiencing sustained memory pressure that will slow performance. The right reaction is to find leaking processes or add memory, not merely to clear caches. A practical approach: run free -h to check available memory, then vmstat to see if si/so values are elevated; if swap activity is high, find the process consuming memory and consider restarting or optimizing it. Be mindful that aggressive monitoring intervals can themselves affect behavior; collect short samples during investigation and avoid long-running, resource-heavy sampling on production hosts.

Disk issues often show up as full filesystems or as slow input and output that makes applications wait. Start with df -h to find filesystems that are nearly full; a full root filesystem can prevent services from writing logs and crash processes. Look at r/s and w/s to see read and write request rates and %util to see how saturated the device is. A common misconception is equating large file counts with slow input and output; the device's utilization and average wait time are the real indicators. After identifying a busy device, inspect which processes are performing heavy input and output and consider throttling, scheduling, or moving data off the device. Remember that heavy monitoring itself can produce additional input and output, so use short, targeted sampling intervals when diagnosing production systems.

Network performance problems can mimic other bottlenecks, so include a network check in your diagnostic flow. Remember that iftop and similar tools are not always installed by default and may require privileges; use them briefly on production systems to reduce tool overhead. Correlate network findings with application logs to determine whether slowness originates from networking or from a busy backend.
